sentences.text: The text defines yoga in one short sūtra: yogaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ, 'yoga is the restriction of the fluctuations of mind-stuff' (Woods), which Vivekananda renders as restraining the mind-stuff from taking various forms.

Johnston's version differs: he reads 1.2 as 'Union' gained through control of the psychic nature, which makes yoga the result of the control, whereas the Sanskrit equates yoga with the restriction (nirodha) itself.
When the fluctuations are restricted, the Seer abides in its own nature, and at other times it takes the same form as the fluctuations.
The fluctuations to be restricted are five: valid ideas, misconception, predicate-relation (vikalpa), sleep and memory.
Their restriction comes through practice and passionlessness, where practice is repeated exertion to keep the mind-stuff established in the restricted state.
The edition's later teaching on the eight aids, ending in samādhi, and on seedless concentration can be read as the fuller working-out of this definition, though 1.2 itself does not say so.
Yoga is defined as the restriction of the fluctuations (vṛttis) of the mind-stuff (citta).
The text names the two means directly: the restriction of these fluctuations comes through abhyāsa (practice) and vairāgya (passionlessness, or non-attachment).

Practice is repeated exertion so that the mind-stuff becomes established in the restricted state, and it becomes firmly confirmed when cultivated for a long time, without interruption, and with earnest attention.
Vairāgya is the consciousness of mastery in one who has lost thirst for objects, whether seen or revealed (heard of).
Its highest form comes from discernment of the Self and brings thirstlessness even for the guṇas (qualities).

Johnston translates abhyāsa and vairāgya freely as 'right use of the will' and 'ceasing from self-indulgence', whereas Woods and Vivekananda stay closer to the Sanskrit with 'practice' and 'passionlessness/non-attachment', so the Sanskrit supports the latter.

The fluctuations (vṛtti) of mind-stuff are said to be of five kinds, and each kind is either hindered or unhindered (Vivekananda: painful or not painful; Johnston ties 'hindered' to the five hindrances).
The five are: sources of valid ideas (pramāṇa), misconception (viparyaya), predicate-relation or conceptual construction (vikalpa), sleep (nidrā), and memory (smṛti).
The valid sources are perception, inference, and verbal communication (Vivekananda: 'competent evidence', Johnston: 'trustworthy testimony'), which is the Sanskrit āgama.

Misconception is erroneous knowledge that does not rest on the true form of its object, while vikalpa follows words or perception but has no corresponding object (Vivekananda's 'verbal delusion' and Johnston's 'predication' both render vikalpa).

Sleep is a fluctuation supported by the absence of waking and dreaming contents (Vivekananda: 'voidness'), and memory is not letting a previously experienced object slip away (Woods: 'not-adding-surreptitiously').

Vivekananda's 'right knowledge, indiscrimination' for the first two terms is looser than Woods and Johnston, since the Sanskrit pramāṇa and viparyaya are 'valid source' and 'misconception' or 'unsound intellection'.
The text names three valid sources of knowledge (pramāṇa): perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna) and verbal communication (āgama).
Pramāṇa is the first of the five kinds of mental fluctuation (vṛtti), the others being misconception, predicate-relation (vikalpa), sleep and memory.

The translators render āgama differently: Woods has 'verbal-communication', Johnston 'trustworthy testimony', and Vivekananda 'competent evidence'; the Sanskrit word itself does not specify who counts as trustworthy or competent.
Misconception is false knowledge that does not rest on the true form of its object, so it is set apart from valid knowledge.

The text says that insight arising in the state of concentration has a different object from insight gained through hearing (śruta) or inference, because its object is a particular, so it presents that insight as going beyond these ordinary sources.

Vivekananda's gloss that testimony and inference concern 'common objects' and that this higher knowledge penetrates where they cannot is an interpretation, since the Sanskrit only says the object is a particular (viśeṣa).

answer.note: Woods and Vivekananda keep Īśvara as a distinct term (Vivekananda also renders it 'God' and 'Supreme Ruler'). Johnston renders it 'the Master'. The Sanskrit in 1.24 defines Īśvara as a 'special puruṣa', which Woods and Vivekananda follow closely. Johnston's 'the spiritual man' loses the word 'special'.

sentences.text: Īśvara is defined as a special kind of puruṣa (Self), untouched by the hindrances, by karmas, by their fruition, and by latent deposits.
In Īśvara the germ of omniscience, which exists in others only as a seed, is at its utmost excellence.
Īśvara is also teacher of the earliest teachers, because He is not limited by time, and His expressing word is the mystic syllable praṇava (Om).
Repeating Om and reflecting on its meaning is prescribed, which links the word to Īśvara as an object of practice.
Īśvara is also a practical focus: devotion (īśvarapraṇidhāna) is an alternative route to concentration, a part of kriyā-yoga, one of the observances, and a source of perfected samādhi.

Since Īśvara is a puruṣa free from the hindrances and karma that the text elsewhere ties to the Self's bondage, Īśvara can be read as a standing example of the freedom the text aims at, though the sūtras do not say this directly.
The word that expresses Īśvara is the praṇava, the mystic syllable OM; Woods calls it 'the Mystic-syllable', while Johnston and Vivekananda name it directly as OM.
This is the Īśvara described as a special kind of Self (puruṣa), untouched by hindrances, karmas, their fruition and latent deposits.
What is to be done with it is repetition (japa) of the word together with reflection on its meaning; Johnston adds that the repetition should be soundless.
Because the word expresses Īśvara, reflecting on its meaning can be read as a form of the devotion to Īśvara (īśvarapraṇidhāna) through which concentration is said to be attained.

The text says that from this practice come the right knowledge of the inward-turned consciousness (Woods: 'of him who thinks in an inverse way'; Johnston: 'interior consciousness'; Vivekananda: 'introspection') and the removal of obstacles.

Sūtra 1.30 lists the obstacles (antarāyāḥ) as the distractions of the mind-stuff: sickness, languor or inertia, doubt, heedlessness, worldliness or laziness, erroneous perception, failure to attain any stage of concentration, and instability once a stage is reached.

The translators render several terms differently: Woods has 'heedlessness' and 'worldliness' where Johnston has 'lightmindedness', 'laziness' and 'intemperance', and Vivekananda has 'lack of enthusiasm' and 'clinging to sense-enjoyments'; the Sanskrit terms pramāda, ālasya and avirati are the basis for these varying choices.
Sūtra 1.31 adds accompaniments of these distractions: pain or grief, despondency, unsteadiness or tremor of the body, and irregular inhalation and exhalation.
The text offers remedies: practice upon a single entity, and cultivating friendliness, compassion, joy and indifference toward happiness, pain, merit and demerit.
Elsewhere, thoughts arising from subliminal impressions are said to appear in the intervals of the concentrated mind, and these can also be read as interruptions.
Sūtra 3.37 calls the supernormal powers obstacles in concentration, though they are perfections in the emergent state.
Sūtra 1.33 says the mind (citta) becomes clear and calm through cultivating four attitudes: friendliness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), joy (muditā) and indifference (upekṣā).
Each attitude is matched to a kind of object: friendliness to happiness, compassion to pain, joy to merit, and indifference to demerit.

Woods is closest to the Sanskrit here, and Johnston's wording is freer: he gives 'sympathy with the happy', 'delight in the holy' and 'disregard of the unholy', and he renders the result as the psychic nature moving to 'gracious peace'.
Vivekananda's 'Friendship, mercy, gladness, and indifference' and his 'pacify the Chitta' stay near the Sanskrit's cittaprasādanam, which means making the mind clear or serene.
This practice appears among the means offered for steadying a mind disturbed by the distractions listed in the preceding sūtras, such as pain, despondency and doubt.
Seedless samādhi (nirbīja samādhi) is reached when the subliminal impression born of the highest seeded state is itself restricted, so that everything is restricted.
The seeded concentrations are the balanced states (samāpatti) described earlier, which include those with and without deliberation or reflection, and the sūtras name them 'seeded' samādhi.

The last of these, the clear super-reflective state, leaves a truth-bearing insight and an impression that is hostile to other impressions, and it is this impression that is restricted in seedless samādhi.

The other concentration, not conscious of objects, rests only on subliminal impressions and follows the practice that brings cessation of fluctuations. Whether this is the same as seedless samādhi is not stated outright, so linking 1.18 to 1.51 is an interpretation.
Even attention, contemplation and concentration held together (saṃyama) are said to be only indirect (external) aids to the seedless state.

The translators differ on 1.51: Johnston calls it 'pure spiritual consciousness' with no seed of separateness left, while Woods and Vivekananda keep the plainer 'seedless concentration' (samādhi) that the Sanskrit nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ supports.

Kriyā-yoga is made up of three practices: tapas (Woods: self-castigation; Vivekananda: mortification; Johnston: fervent aspiration), svādhyāya (study or spiritual reading), and īśvara-praṇidhāna (devotion to Īśvara).

The Sanskrit names devotion to Īśvara, which Woods renders as devotion and Johnston as complete obedience to the Master, whereas Vivekananda adds 'surrendering fruits of work', a gloss that goes beyond the wording of the sūtra.
Its stated purpose is twofold: the cultivation of samādhi and the attenuation of the kleśas (hindrances).

The kleśas are avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa and abhiniveśa (Woods: undifferentiated-consciousness, the feeling-of-personality, passion, aversion, the will-to-live), so kriyā-yoga is aimed at thinning these five.
The same three practices recur in the niyamas, where devotion to Īśvara is said to bring perfection of samādhi, so one can read kriyā-yoga as a compact form of the practice that leads toward samādhi.

Since the kleśas are also the root of the karmic deposit, thinning them can be read as part of the larger aim of ending pain and bondage, which the text describes as the cessation of the kleśas and karma.
Sūtra 2.3 names the five kleśas (hindrances, or pain-bearing obstructions): avidyā, asmitā, rāga, dveṣa and abhiniveśa.

Woods renders these as undifferentiated-consciousness (avidyā), the feeling-of-personality, passion, aversion and the will-to-live; Johnston gives unwisdom, self-assertion, lust, hate and attachment; Vivekananda gives ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion and clinging to life.

The translations differ most on the fifth term: Johnston's "attachment" and Vivekananda's "attachment" for rāga blur the two, whereas the Sanskrit and Woods separate rāga (passion, dwelling on pleasure) from abhiniveśa (the will-to-live, which Johnston also glosses as desire toward life).

Avidyā is the recognition of the permanent, pure, pleasurable and self in what is impermanent, impure, painful and not-self, and it is the field for the other four whether they are dormant, attenuated, intercepted or sustained.

Asmitā is the appearance of the power of seeing and the instrument of seeing as a single self; rāga dwells on pleasure, dveṣa dwells on pain, and abhiniveśa flows on by its own nature even in the wise.
These hindrances are to be attenuated by kriyāyoga and, once subtle, escaped by inverse-propagation, and their cessation follows the rain-cloud concentration.
Avidyā is listed first among the five hindrances (kleśas), the others being the feeling-of-personality (asmitā), passion, aversion and the will-to-live.
The text defines avidyā directly as recognizing the permanent, the pure, pleasure and a self in what is actually impermanent, impure, pain and not-self.

Woods renders avidyā as 'undifferentiated-consciousness', Johnston as 'the darkness of unwisdom', and Vivekananda as 'ignorance'; all three give the same definition in 2.5, so the difference is one of wording, not of meaning.
Avidyā is called the field (kṣetra) of the other hindrances, whether they are dormant, attenuated, intercepted or sustained.
It is also named as the cause of the correlation (saṃyoga) of the Seer and the object-of-sight, which is itself the cause of what is to be escaped.

Reading these together, avidyā is a systematic mistaking of one kind of thing for its opposite, and it is the root condition that liberation (kaivalya) must remove, with unwavering discriminative discernment as the means.
The pain to be avoided is the pain that has not yet come, and its cause is the correlation (saṃyoga) of the Seer and the object-of-sight; Johnston reads this as the Seer's absorption in things seen.

The reason for that correlation is avidyā (undifferentiated-consciousness, or ignorance), which means taking the impermanent, impure, painful and not-self to be permanent, pure, pleasant and the Self.
Avidyā is the field for the other four hindrances (kleśas): the feeling of personality (asmitā), passion, aversion and the will-to-live.
These hindrances are the root of the latent deposit of karma, which ripens as birth, life-span and experience, and these bring joy or anguish according to merit or demerit.
Read together, the text points to ignorance as the deepest cause: it sustains the Seer's identification with the mind's fluctuations (1.4) and so with the hindrances and karma that bear pain.
When avidyā ends, the correlation ends and the Seer is isolated, and the hindrances and karma then cease.
Sūtra 2.29 names eight limbs (aṅgāni) of yoga: yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna and samādhi.

The first two are defined as the yamas (non-injury, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence, non-acceptance of gifts) and the niyamas (cleanliness, contentment, self-castigation or austerity, study, and devotion to Īśvara).
Āsana is a posture that is stable and easy, and prāṇāyāma is the cutting off of the flow of inhalation and exhalation, which follows once posture is stable.
Pratyāhāra is the senses disjoining from their objects and, as it were, imitating the mind-stuff.

Dhāraṇā is binding the mind to a place, dhyāna is a focused, unbroken holding of the idea on that place, and samādhi is that same contemplation shining forth as only the object and, as it were, empty of itself.

The text calls the last three together saṃyama and treats them as more inward than the first five, though still outer aids to seedless samādhi; Johnston's term "Contemplation" for samādhi in 2.29 differs from Woods's "concentration", but the Sanskrit samādhi is the same in both.
The yamas are the first of the eight aids (aṅgas) of yoga.
Sūtra 2.30 lists the five yamas: ahiṃsā (non-injury), satya (truthfulness), asteya (non-stealing), brahmacarya (continence), and aparigraha.

The translations differ on aparigraha: Woods renders it as abstinence from acceptance of gifts, Vivekananda as non-receiving, and Johnston as abstaining from covetousness, so the Sanskrit term can be read either as not accepting or as not coveting.
Johnston and Vivekananda render brahmacarya as impurity-avoidance or continence, and Woods as abstinence from incontinence.
The yamas are called the Great Course-of-conduct (mahāvrata) when they are unqualified by species, place, time or exigency.
Each yama is later said to bear a result when firmly established, for example the cessation of enmity near one grounded in ahiṃsā and the acquiring of energy through brahmacarya.
The niyamas are the second of the eight limbs (aṅga) of yoga, listed right after the yamas.

Sūtra 2.32 names five: śauca (cleanliness or purity), saṃtoṣa (contentment), tapas (self-castigation, or fervent aspiration in Johnston), svādhyāya (study, or spiritual reading), and īśvarapraṇidhāna (devotion to Īśvara).

The translators differ on wording here: Woods renders tapas as 'self-castigation' and Vivekananda as 'mortification', while Johnston's 'fervent aspiration' is softer, and the Sanskrit word itself is the same in all three.
Vivekananda adds 'internal and external' to purification, and Johnston calls īśvarapraṇidhāna 'perfect obedience to the Master'; Woods' 'devotion to the Īśvara' stays closer to the Sanskrit.
The last three niyamas (tapas, svādhyāya, īśvarapraṇidhāna) also appear together as kriyā-yoga, which aims at samādhi and at thinning the hindrances (kleśas).

The text links each niyama to a result: purity brings disgust at one's own body and non-intercourse with others, contentment brings superlative pleasure, tapas brings perfection of body and organs, study brings communion with the chosen deity, and devotion to Īśvara brings perfection of concentration.
The text says that once a yogin is grounded in abstinence from injury (ahiṃsā), enmity is suspended in his presence.
Woods says his presence begets a suspension of enmity, and Johnston and Vivekananda say all enmity ceases in the presence of one in whom non-injury is perfected or established.
The Sanskrit (tatsaṃnidhau vairatyāgaḥ) points to the abandonment of hostility near him, so the effect is placed in those around the yogin as much as in the yogin himself.
Ahiṃsā is the first of the five yamas, which are non-injury, truthfulness, non-stealing, continence and non-acceptance of gifts.
The yamas are called the Great Course-of-conduct (mahāvrata) when they are not limited by species, place, time or exigency.
The edition gives no further result of ahiṃsā being established beyond this suspension of enmity.
Posture (āsana) is defined as sthira-sukham: stable and easy, or firm and pleasant.
Johnston renders this as 'firm and without strain', which is a freer wording, while Woods and Vivekananda stay closer to the Sanskrit's pairing of steadiness with ease or pleasantness.
It is gained by relaxation of effort and by a state of balance, or meditation, on Ananta, the unlimited.

Johnston reads the effort as 'steady and temperate' and the object as 'the everlasting', and Vivekananda reads it as lessening the tendency to restlessness, so the translators differ on how the effort is to be understood.
The result of a mastered posture is that one is unassailed by extremes (dvandva), the pairs of opposites.
Posture is the third of the eight aids to yoga, and stability of posture is what the restraint of breath follows from.
Prāṇāyāma is the fourth of the eight aids (aṅgas) of yoga, listed after abstentions, observances and posture and before withdrawal of the senses.
It is defined as the cutting off or control of the flow of inhalation and exhalation, and it follows once a stable, easy posture has been gained.

It may be external, internal, or suppressed, is regulated by place, time and number, and is prolonged and subtle; Vivekananda renders the last quality as 'long or short', but the Sanskrit (dīrghasūkṣmaḥ) and Woods support 'protracted and subtile'.

A fourth kind transcends the external and internal objects, though Vivekananda reads it as restraining prāṇa by reflecting on an external or internal object, which is not what Woods and Johnston give.
Its results are that the covering of the light dwindles away and the mind becomes fit for fixed attention (dhāraṇā).
Elsewhere, expulsion and retention of breath is named as one way the mind may reach calm, and irregular breathing is listed as an accompaniment of mental distraction.
Withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) is the fifth of the eight aids or limbs of yoga, listed after the regulations of breath and before fixed attention.

Sūtra 2.54 defines it as the organs disjoining themselves from their own objects and, as it were, imitating the mind-stuff as it is in itself (Woods); Vivekananda has the organs giving up their objects and taking the form of the mind-stuff, as it were.

Johnston's wording is freer, describing it as disengaging the powers from entanglement in outer things as the psychic nature is withdrawn and stilled, but the Sanskrit (svaviṣayāsaṃprayoge, cittasvarūpānukāra iva) supports the closer reading that the senses cease to engage their objects and follow the mind.
The result stated is supreme mastery of the organs.

Read together with the sūtra on the mind's fitness for fixed attention (dhāraṇā), withdrawal appears to prepare the ground for the later inner limbs, which begin with binding the mind-stuff to a place.
Dhāraṇā is binding the mind-stuff to a place; Vivekananda renders this as holding the mind on to a particular object, and Johnston calls it attention.
Dhyāna is the focusedness of the presented idea on that same place; Vivekananda calls it an unbroken flow of knowledge in the object, and Johnston a prolonged holding there.

Samādhi is that same contemplation shining forth as the intended object alone, as if emptied of itself; Johnston adds 'freed from the sense of separateness and personality', which goes beyond the Sanskrit's 'svarūpaśūnyam iva'.

So the three can be read as successive deepenings on one object: fixing the mind, sustaining a single stream on it, and then only the object's meaning appearing, with the mind seeming empty of itself.
When all three are practiced together on one object, this is called saṃyama.
They are listed as the sixth, seventh and eighth limbs of yoga, and are more inward than the earlier five limbs, though still outer aids to seedless concentration.
Saṃyama is defined as the three in one: dhāraṇā, dhyāna and samādhi practiced together on a single object.

Those three are defined as binding the mind-stuff to a place (dhāraṇā), focusedness of the presented idea on it (dhyāna), and the same state shining forth as the object alone, as if emptied of itself (samādhi).

Woods renders saṃyama as "constraint" and Johnston as "perfectly concentrated Meditation", while Vivekananda leaves it as Samyama; the Sanskrit trayam ekatra saṃyamaḥ simply says the three are at one place or object.
Mastering saṃyama brings the shining forth of insight, and it is to be applied by stages.
Saṃyama is then directed at various objects, such as the three mutations, which gives knowledge of past and future, or the sun, which gives knowledge of the cosmic spaces.
The three that make up saṃyama are inner aids compared with the earlier five limbs, yet they remain indirect aids to seedless concentration.

answer.note: The edition treats the powers (siddhis, vibhūtis) as ambivalent: they are real results of saṃyama, but they are obstacles to the highest concentration and should be renounced for liberation.

sentences.text: The text describes many powers that arise from saṃyama, such as knowledge of past and future, invisibility, mastery of the elements, and the bodily perfections of aṇimā and the rest.

Woods says these powers are obstacles in concentration (samādhi) but perfections in the emergent, worldly state; Vivekananda agrees, while Johnston only says they stand in contradistinction to the highest spiritual vision.
The yogin is told to feel no attachment or pride when high beings invite him, because undesired consequences recur.
Isolation (kaivalya) comes through passionlessness even toward these perfections, once the seeds of defects have dwindled.
So the powers help only as signs of mastery or in the worldly state, and for the goal of kaivalya they are something to be given up rather than relied on.
The text also notes that such perfections can arise by birth, drugs, spells, self-castigation or concentration, and only the one born of contemplation leaves no latent deposit.

Kaivalya is the outcome of the ending of avidyā: when that ignorance does not exist there is no saṃyoga (correlation) of Seer and seen, and this is the escape, called Isolation by Woods and 'the independence of the seer' by Vivekananda.

Johnston renders 2.25 as 'attainment of his own pure being' and 'great liberation', which is looser than the Sanskrit; the word kaivalya itself is clearest in Woods's 'Isolation' and Vivekananda's 'independence'.
It is reached when the sattva and the Self are equally pure (3.55), and also after the yogin turns away even from the powers and the seeds of defects dwindle (3.50).
The means is unwavering discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti), and the mind-stuff that has become inclined toward discrimination is described as moving onward toward Kaivalya.

The final sūtra defines it in two ways: as the inverse resolution (pratiprasava) of the guṇas, which no longer serve a purpose for the Self, or as the power of pure consciousness (citi-śakti) established in its own nature.
Read together, these suggest that kaivalya is the Seer abiding in its own nature, apart from the entanglement with mind and nature that 1.3 and 1.4 describe.

answer.note: The edition names dharmamegha samādhi only in 4.29 and describes it mainly through its conditions and its results in 4.30-4.32. It gives no further definition of the term itself.

sentences.text: Dharmamegha samādhi is named in 4.29 as a concentration that follows from discriminative discernment (vivekakhyāti) in every case.
The sūtra says it comes to one who is "not usurious" even toward prasaṃkhyāna (Woods: "Elevation"). Johnston reads this as being wholly free from self, and Vivekananda as giving up the fruits.

The translators render the name differently: Woods has "Rain-cloud of [knowable] things", Johnston "gathered together like a cloud", and Vivekananda "cloud of virtue". Since the Sanskrit gives dharma-megha, "cloud of dharma", Woods's "things" and Vivekananda's "virtue" are two different readings of dharma.
Its first stated result is the cessation of the hindrances (kleśa) and of karma.
The next result is that knowledge, freed from all obscuring defilements, becomes endless, so that little remains to be known.
After this the guṇas have fulfilled their purpose and reach the end of their sequence of mutations, which the text then connects with kaivalya (Isolation).

answer.note: The word 'chakra' does not appear as a doctrine or system in this edition. Three sūtras name bodily sites for concentration, and only 3.29 uses the word cakra, in nābhicakra. The text does not list a set of chakras, number them, or describe energy centres in a system.

sentences.text: Sūtra 3.29 says that constraint (saṃyama) upon the nābhicakra, the 'wheel of the navel', brings knowledge of the arrangement of the body.
Woods translates cakra as 'wheel' and Vivekananda as 'navel circle', while Johnston renders it as 'the centre of force in the lower trunk', which adds an interpretation not in the Sanskrit wording.

Sūtra 3.30 names the 'well of the throat' (kaṇṭhakūpa) as a site of constraint that brings cessation of hunger and thirst, and Johnston again calls it a 'centre of force'; the Sanskrit word used there is kūpa ('well'), not cakra.
Other sites of concentration named are the radiance in the head (3.32) and the heart (3.34), but neither is called a cakra.
Reading these together, the text uses bodily locations as objects of saṃyama with specific results, but it does not present them as a connected system of chakras.

answer.note: The edition names posture (āsana) as the third limb of yoga and defines it only by quality, as stable and easy. It names no specific postures, so headstand, lotus or any other pose is not mentioned.

sentences.text: Posture (āsana) is listed as the third of the eight limbs of yoga, after the abstentions and observances and before breath regulation.
The only definition given is a quality: posture is stable and easy (Woods), firm and without strain (Johnston), or firm and pleasant (Vivekananda).

The next sūtra says it is perfected by relaxing effort and by a balanced mental state toward Ananta (Woods), or by setting the heart upon the everlasting (Johnston), or by meditating on the unlimited (Vivekananda). Again, this concerns how to sit, not which shape to take.
The text says that when posture is mastered, one is unassailed by extremes, and that breath restraint follows once posture is stable.
Reading these together, the criterion is stability and ease rather than any named pose, so the text leaves the choice of posture open.

answer.note: The edition has no sūtra on food or diet: it names no foods, meal rules, or fasting. It touches the topic only in a few places. One sūtra says that a particular meditation brings cessation of hunger and thirst, and another lists self-indulgence and intemperance in broader terms.

sentences.text: Constraint on the 'well of the throat' is said to bring the cessation of hunger and thirst, but this is a result of meditative practice and not a rule about what to eat.

Johnston lists 'intemperance' among the obstacles to interior consciousness, while Woods has 'worldliness' and Vivekananda has 'clinging to sense-enjoyments', so the Sanskrit's wider sense of non-abstinence should not be read narrowly as eating habits.
Passionlessness is described as mastery over thirst for seen or revealed objects, which is a general teaching on non-attachment and does not mention food.
The observances include cleanliness and contentment, and the text states no dietary application of either.

answer.note: This edition never mentions kuṇḍalinī, a coiled energy, or its awakening or rising. Its nearest material is a few sūtras on constraint (saṃyama) upon bodily centres, and on mastery of the vital currents (Udāna, Samāna), none of which are linked to kuṇḍalinī.

sentences.text: Sūtra 3.29 names constraint upon the 'wheel of the navel' (nābhicakra) as giving knowledge of the arrangement of the body, but it says nothing of an energy that rises.
Sūtras 3.30 and 3.31 name constraint upon the well of the throat and upon the tortoise-tube (kūrmanāḍī), with the results of ending hunger and thirst and of steadiness.
Sūtra 3.32 names constraint upon the radiance in the head, which gives the sight of the Siddhas, and 3.34 names constraint upon the heart, which gives knowledge of the mind-stuff.
Sūtras 3.39 and 3.40 describe mastery of the Udāna and Samāna currents, with results of ascension and radiance.
These are the closest points of contact, but the text does not connect any of them to kuṇḍalinī, so any such link would come from outside this edition.

answer.note: The edition never mentions Krishna. It does teach about Īśvara, a special Puruṣa, and devotion to him, but nothing in the sūtras identifies Īśvara with Krishna, and saying so would require outside knowledge.

sentences.text: The sūtras speak of Īśvara (the Master or Supreme Ruler), described as a special kind of Self untouched by hindrances, karma, its fruition and latent deposits.
In Īśvara the germ of omniscience is at its utmost, and he is teacher even of the earliest sages because time does not limit him.
His expressing word is the mystic syllable Om, to be repeated with reflection on its meaning.
Devotion to Īśvara is offered as a means to concentration and is counted within the yoga of action and the observances.
Study is said to bring communion with the chosen deity, but the text does not name that deity.
